title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text: Adopt a URL-based API versioning strategy (/v1/, /v2/) for all public-facing platform APIs, with a defined deprecation lifecycle.

title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text: Adopt a URL-based API versioning strategy (/v1/, /v2/) for all public-facing platform APIs, with a defined deprecation lifecycle.

title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text:
Motivation
As the platform grows, breaking changes to APIs are inevitable. Without a clear versioning strategy, clients break unexpectedly and the team lacks guidance on when and how to evolve APIs.
Goals:

Give consumers clear, stable API contracts
Provide a migration path when breaking changes are necessary
Establish a deprecation timeline so old versions don’t live forever

title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text:
Detailed Design

Versioning Scheme
All public APIs include a version prefix in the URL path:
https://api.example.com/v1/resources
https://api.example.com/v2/resources


Version Lifecycle





stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Current
    Current --> Supported : New major version released
    Supported --> Deprecated : 12 months
    Deprecated --> Removed : 6 months
    Removed --> [*]

    Current : Actively developed
    Current : Receives all fixes
    Supported : Security & critical fixes only
    Deprecated : No fixes, Sunset header
    Removed : Returns 410 Gone














Phase
Duration
Description




Current
Ongoing
Actively developed, receives all fixes


Supported
12 months
Receives security and critical bug fixes


Deprecated
6 months
No fixes, returns Sunset header


Removed
—
Returns 410 Gone





Breaking Change Definition
A breaking change is any modification that could cause existing clients to fail:

Removing or renaming a field
Changing a field type
Removing an endpoint
Changing authentication requirements

Non-breaking changes (adding fields, new endpoints) do not require a version bump.


Implementation





graph TD
    Client([Client]) -->|/v1/resources| GW[API Gateway]
    Client -->|/v2/resources| GW

    GW --> V1[v1 Handler]
    GW --> V2[v2 Handler]

    V1 --> Shared[Shared Business Logic]
    V2 --> Shared
    Shared --> DB[(Database)]







API gateway routes requests to the correct version handler
Each version is a separate module/package in the codebase
Shared business logic lives in version-independent modules

title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text:
Alternatives Considered

Header-based versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json): Harder to discover and test; URL-based is more explicit.
No versioning: Unacceptable for a platform with external consumers.
Query parameter versioning (?version=1): Non-standard and easily overlooked.

title: RFC-0002: API Versioning Strategy
text:
Open Questions

Should internal service-to-service APIs follow the same versioning scheme, or is this only for external APIs?
What tooling do we need for automated compatibility checking between versions?

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text: Design a standardized CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions that supports monorepo builds, parallel testing, and automated deployments to staging and production environments.

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text: Design a standardized CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions that supports monorepo builds, parallel testing, and automated deployments to staging and production environments.

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text:
Motivation
Current CI/CD is fragmented: some services use Jenkins, others use ad-hoc GitHub Actions workflows, and deployment processes are manual. This leads to:

Inconsistent build and test practices across teams
Slow feedback loops (some pipelines take 30+ minutes)
Manual, error-prone deployments

A unified pipeline will standardize how code is built, tested, and deployed.

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text:
Detailed Design

Pipeline Stages





graph LR
    Commit([Commit]) --> Lint[Lint]
    Commit --> Test[Unit Test]
    Lint --> Build[Build]
    Test --> Build
    Build --> DeployStg[Deploy Staging]
    DeployStg --> IntTest[Integration Test]
    IntTest --> Gate{Manual\nApproval}
    Gate -->|Approved| DeployProd[Deploy Prod]
    Gate -->|Rejected| Stop([Stop])

    style Gate fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#664d03
    style DeployProd fill:#d1e7dd,stroke:#0f5132
    style Stop fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#842029








Change Detection
For the monorepo, the pipeline detects which services changed and only builds/tests those:
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'services/auth/**'
      - 'services/api/**'
      - 'libs/shared/**'
Changes to libs/shared/ trigger builds for all dependent services.





graph TD
    Shared[libs/shared] --> Auth[services/auth]
    Shared --> API[services/api]
    Shared --> Billing[services/billing]

    Auth --> AuthBuild[Build Auth]
    API --> APIBuild[Build API]
    Billing --> BillingBuild[Build Billing]

    style Shared fill:#cff4fc,stroke:#055160








Parallel Execution

Linting and unit tests run in parallel across all affected services
Integration tests run after all service builds complete
Deployment is sequential: staging first, then production after approval



Environment Promotion



Environment
Trigger
Approval




Staging
Push to main
Automatic


Production
Staging tests pass
Manual gate





Caching Strategy

Dependencies: Cache node_modules / Go modules by lockfile hash
Docker layers: Use GitHub Actions cache for Docker build layers
Build artifacts: Cache compiled outputs between stages

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text:
Alternatives Considered

GitLab CI: Would require migrating repositories; GitHub Actions has sufficient capability.
ArgoCD for everything: Better suited for Kubernetes deployments but doesn’t replace CI for build/test stages.
Per-repo pipelines: Simpler initially but leads to drift and duplication across teams.

title: RFC-0001: CI/CD Pipeline Design
text:
Open Questions

Should we use self-hosted runners for performance-sensitive builds, or are GitHub-hosted runners sufficient?
How do we handle database migrations in the pipeline?
What’s the rollback strategy if a production deployment fails?

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text: Introduce a dedicated authentication service to centralize user identity, token issuance, and session management across all platform services.

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text: Introduce a dedicated authentication service to centralize user identity, token issuance, and session management across all platform services.

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text:
Motivation
Authentication logic is currently duplicated across multiple services, leading to inconsistent session handling, duplicated security patches, and difficulty onboarding new services. A centralized auth service will:

Provide a single source of truth for user identity
Standardize token formats (JWT) and validation
Simplify onboarding for new services

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text:
Detailed Design

Architecture
The auth service runs as a standalone microservice exposing REST and gRPC APIs. All services validate tokens by calling the auth service or by verifying JWTs locally using a shared public key.





graph LR
    Client([Client App])
    Auth[Auth Service]
    DB[(User Store)]
    PK[Public Key Cache]

    Client -->|credentials| Auth
    Auth -->|query| DB
    Auth -->|issue JWT| Client

    Client -->|request + JWT| SvcA[Service A]
    Client -->|request + JWT| SvcB[Service B]

    SvcA -->|verify signature| PK
    SvcB -->|verify signature| PK
    Auth -.->|publish public key| PK








Token Flow





sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant AuthService
    participant UserStore
    participant APIService

    Client->>AuthService: POST /auth/login (credentials)
    AuthService->>UserStore: Validate credentials
    UserStore-->>AuthService: User record
    AuthService-->>Client: Access token (15 min) + Refresh token (7 days)

    Client->>APIService: Request + Access token
    APIService->>APIService: Verify JWT signature
    APIService-->>Client: Response

    Note over Client,AuthService: When access token expires...
    Client->>AuthService: POST /auth/refresh (refresh token)
    AuthService-->>Client: New access token








API Endpoints



Endpoint
Method
Description




/auth/login
POST
Authenticate user


/auth/refresh
POST
Refresh access token


/auth/logout
POST
Revoke refresh token


/auth/verify
GET
Verify token validity





Data Model

users: id, email, password_hash, created_at, updated_at
refresh_tokens: id, user_id, token_hash, expires_at, revoked_at



Rate Limiting
To protect against brute-force attacks, the auth service enforces rate limits on authentication endpoints:



Endpoint
Limit
Window




/auth/login
10 attempts
15 min


/auth/refresh
30 requests
1 min


/auth/verify
100 requests
1 min



After exceeding the limit, the service returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text:
Alternatives Considered

Shared library approach: Distributing auth as a library was considered but rejected due to version drift and the inability to revoke sessions centrally.
Third-party auth (Auth0, Firebase): Adds external dependency and cost; we need tighter integration with our user model.

title: RFC-0001: Authentication Service
text:
Open Questions

Should we support OAuth2 for third-party integrations in v1? Decided: No, defer to v2.
